title: Topology-sensitive profiling guide — Llama / Mistral / Qwen (long-context + MoE)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working checklist + pattern library for topology-sensitive profiling when investigating long-context behaviour and MoE routing differences across Llama, Mistral, and Qwen model variants. The aim is pragmatic: reproducible steps to isolate where latency and jitter come from when request populations include long-window sessions and when routing creates uneven expert fanout.

Context and goals:
- We observe sporadic 2–5x tail latency spikes on long-context workloads (8k+ tokens) on Dedicated pools with mixed model catalogs (Llama 70B, Mistral 22B, Qwen 15B).
- Hypotheses: (1) routing topology and inter-GPU comms (NVLink/PCIe) amplify MoE fanout variance; (2) KV-cache layout and prefix sharing cause fragmentation in batching; (3) certain attention/chunking paths trigger expensive CUDA kernels for specific architectures.
- Goals: create repeatable microtrace patterns, quantify contribution slices (kernel time vs comms vs serialization), and produce targeted mitigations (topology pinning, split-batch heuristics, prefetched-KV strategies).

Quick summary of recommended approach:
1) Recreate the tail-case with synthetic workload that mimics real prefix reuse and size skew (80/20 session length distribution).
2) Collect microtraces: nsight-cu-profiler + perfetto on host, and an application-level ordered event stream (enqueue, route, serialize, cuda-launch, nvlink-send, nvlink-wait, cuda-sync).
3) Correlate gating decisions (expert indices per request) with fanout patterns and NVLink heatmaps.
4) Compare per-layer latency breakdown across architectures and across routing topologies (ring/hub/flat). See sections below for commands and expected signatures.

Synthetic workload recipe (repro steps):
- Use session generator that samples length from a log-normal (mu=7, sigma=1.2) clipped to [64,16384]. Prefix sharing: 30% of sessions share same 2k token prefix to trigger KV reuse.
- Target mix: 60% Llama-70B (dense), 30% Mistral-22B (dense but different attention kernel shapes), 10% Qwen-MoE variant (2-expert-per-token routing).
- Run 10k requests in 1 minute bursts with concurrency 128 per GPU to expose queueing.

Tracing checklist (minimal set):
- Host: perfetto trace with raw timestamps for enqueue/serialize/worker-pickup/finish.
- GPU: nsight-cu-trace to capture kernel timelines, memory copy and nvlink transfers. Capture 3 bursts per run.
- Application: emit JSON microtrace lines for: request_id, session_id, routing_decision([expert_ids]), batch_id, enqueue_ts, cuda_launch_ts, cuda_sync_ts, kv_hits, serialized_size_bytes.

Example command snippets:
- perfetto: perfetto --config perfetto/long-window-llama.prototxt -o /tmp/trace.pb
- nsight: ncu --set full -o /tmp/ncu.llama70b --target-processes all --trace cdp --nvtx
- runtime microtrace: ./bin/runner --workload workloads/long_window_moe.yaml --emit-trace /tmp/micro.jsonl

Topological experiments to run (design patterns):
- Flat routing (all GPUs equal): baseline. Expect more NVLink scatter but simpler scheduling.
- Hub-and-spoke: designate 1 leader aggregator per rack; route experts to leader to reduce many-to-many transfers. Watch leader hot spots.
- Ring-forwarded routing: route via ring to balance NVLink pairs; this increases latency for larger fanout but can improve aggregate throughput.

What to look for in traces (signatures):
- Batch fragmentation: repeated small cuda-launch kernels with tiny batch sizes interleaved with long nvlink-wait periods. Signature = many <2ms kernels separated by >5ms transfer stalls.
- Expert-hot leader contention: single GPU kernel time low but queue wait large and nvlink-send counts >= number_of_request_peers.
- Kernel size mismatch across architectures: Mistral often shows many small attention kernels due to its attention tiling; Llama exhibits larger fused kernels. Qwen-MoE shows alternating dense and scattered small expert kernels.
- KV-cache rehydrate penalty: when prefix reuse is high but the cache layout spans GPUs, you see nvlink copies of large kv pages (~MB) right before first token scoring.

Quantification matrix (what metrics to compute):
- Per-request latency split: serialization, routing decision, gpu-queue-wait, kernel-exec, nvlink-comm, postprocessing.
- Fanout entropy: distribution of number of experts touched per token across window. Report p50/p95/p99.
- KV fetch size per session and number of cross-GPU KV-chunks.
- Kernel occupancy and SM utilization (by model + layer groups).

Preliminary observations (from pilot runs):
- Llama 70B: steady kernel times for decoder FFN but heavy CUDA kernel fusion leads to good SM utilization; tail mostly from nvlink when prefix spans GPUs.
- Mistral 22B: attention tiling causes many small kernels at long window lengths; this multiplies launch overhead and interacts poorly with fragmented batches. Tail appears as kernel-launch jitter rather than NVLink.
- Qwen-MoE (2-expert routing): average throughput high but variance dominated by expert skew; when top-1 routing probability concentrates on a hot expert, that GPU becomes a bottleneck for both compute and NVLink egress.

Mitigation experiments to try (ordered by cost):
- Low-effort: topology pinning for hot experts (pin heavy experts to NVSwitch-local GPUs), increase per-GPU concurrency cap for leader nodes, enable per-request kv-affinity hints so prefix-heavy sessions stay local.
- Mid-effort: implement hub aggregator for MoE fanout (aggregate gating indices centrally and multicast smaller sub-batches) and split large KV pages into small aligned chunks to allow staggered fetches.
- Higher-effort: kernel fusion tuning for small attention tiles (Mistral): coalesce small kernels into layer groups for long-window mode; implement an adaptive launch aggregator in runtime to batch multiple tiny kernels across requests when safe.

Microtrace correlation heuristics (how to attribute):
1) If nvlink-send counts increase immediately after routing decision and before first kernel launch => attribution to KV fetch.
2) If many small kernels appear with idle NVLink => kernel-launch overhead / attention tiling problem.
3) If one GPU has high queue depth while others idle => expert-hot bottleneck.

Checklist for mitigation validation (A/B):
- Run 3x 5-minute bursts with identical seeds for synthetic workload.
- Baseline: flat routing. Collect perfetto + ncu + microtrace.
- Apply mitigation (pin experts or hub aggregator). Repeat same runs.
- Compare p50/p95/p99 request latency, NVLink bytes, and per-GPU queue depth histograms.

Open questions and TODOs:
- Is there a low-overhead way to expose KV-page locality to the scheduler without large metadata overhead? (Marcus investigating data structures, INF-7894).
- Explore adaptive kernel combiner for Mistral tiled attention (Laura prototyping).
- Should we formalize an "expert health" metric so autoscaler can proactively provision temporary burst capacity?

Relevant artifacts and references:
- INF-7894: MoE topology pinning RFC (WIP).
- perfetto trace: perfetto://trace/2025-11-12-llama70b (pilot).
- PR: runtime/pull/462 — staged kv-chunking experiment.

Next immediate actions (this week):
- Generate reproducible synthetic workload (Evelyn) and share workload yaml.
- Marcus: extract nvlink heatmaps and correlate with microtrace routing decisions.
- Laura: prototype kernel aggregation shim for Mistral small-attention tiles and measure launch overhead improvement.

Notes to self: keep checkpoints small and reproducible. Prefer deterministic gating seeds when possible for A/B. If experiment shows improvement, convert the best mitigation into an opt-in runtime flag for Dedicated clusters to allow gradual rollout.

Appendix: lightweight microtrace schema (newline-delimited JSON entries)
{"ts":162,"req":"r1","sess":"s12","route":[2,5],"kv_hits":3,"cuda_launch_ts":170,"cuda_sync_ts":210}

End of doc.
